meno.title: The slave boy's square
meno.intro: Eudoxus draws a square in the dust with his stick: two feet each side. 'Plato asked a boy this once, in Meno's house. Draw me a square with exactly twice this area.'

feedback.none: Draw lines from point to point in the dust. Click a point, then another.
feedback.given: That is the square we started with: two feet by two, four square feet. We want eight.
feedback.four_times: You doubled the side. Count the small squares inside: sixteen, not eight. Four times as large! The boy made the same mistake.
feedback.nine: Three feet a side gives nine square feet. Too big, though closer. And two gives four, too small. So the side lies between two and three: but where?
feedback.other: Count its area carefully. Is it eight?
feedback.double: Look: each small square is cut in half by your line, and four halves lie inside. Four halves of four squares... eight. The side is the diagonal of the first square, a length that no whole number of feet can measure. Yet you found it.

hints: Doubling the side quadruples the area. The answer is bigger than two feet a side, smaller than three.
Draw the diagonal of the little square. What does it cut the square into?
Build a square on four diagonals: join the middle points of the sides of the big four-by-four square.

waterworks.title: Cimon's water
waterworks.intro: Speusippus unrolls a plan of the channels. 'The reading spot is a swamp and the eastern planes are dying. Water divides equally at every open junction. Make it right before my uncle sees.'
hints: At a junction with three open outlets, each gets a third of what arrives. With two, a half.
Closing a gate does not destroy water: if a junction has no open way out, it overflows.
Turn the western pipe toward the grove, then open the eastern gate so the baths don't get half the river.

labels.solved: The water runs where it should. Somewhere upstream, Cimon is pleased.
